name: Moses (traditional attribution of the Torah)
summary: The Pentateuch itself says Moses wrote specific things — the covenant words, the law, a song — and later Scripture calls the whole 'the Book of Moses'. The books are anonymous as wholes and narrate Moses' death. Jewish and Christian tradition holds Mosaic authorship; critical scholarship since the eighteenth century, in Wellhausen's classic statement, sees the Torah as composed from several sources and edited after the exile.

sources.note: Moses' death narrated in the third person
'the Book of Moses'

sources.title: Prolegomena to the History of Israel
sources.author: Julius Wellhausen
sources.note: the classic statement of the documentary hypothesis; English translation, 1885

traditions: Mosaic authorship: Orthodox Judaism, traditional Catholic and evangelical teaching
Composite authorship (J, E, D, P or successive editions): Julius Wellhausen and critical scholarship after him

name: Joshua (Talmudic attribution)
summary: The book names no writer, but says 'Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God' (24:26). The Talmud says Joshua wrote his own book, and that Eleazar the priest completed it after Joshua's death (24:29) and Phinehas after Eleazar's (24:33). Its 'to this day' (4:9 and often) speaks from after the events. Martin Noth (1943) read Joshua to Kings as one Deuteronomistic History, finished in the exile.

traditions: Joshua, completed by Eleazar and Phinehas: Talmudic and traditional view
Part of the Deuteronomistic History, edited in the exile: Martin Noth (1943) and those who follow him

name: Samuel (Talmudic attribution), finished by Gad and Nathan
summary: None of these books names its writer. The Talmud says Samuel wrote his own book, Judges and Ruth, and that Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet finished Samuel after his death. Chronicles says David's acts are written in the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer. Judges' refrain 'In those days there was no king in Israel' and Ruth's closing genealogy down to David were written once there were kings. Martin Noth read Judges and Samuel as part of the Deuteronomistic History; Ruth has been dated anywhere from the monarchy to after the exile.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b (who wrote the books)
Überlieferungsgeschichtliche Studien
sources.author: Martin Noth
sources.note: Joshua to Kings as one Deuteronomistic History

traditions: Samuel, with Gad and Nathan: Talmudic and traditional view
Deuteronomistic History (Judges, Samuel); Ruth of uncertain date: Martin Noth (1943) and those who follow him

name: Kings: writer unknown (the Talmud says Jeremiah)
summary: Kings names its sources, the Book of the Acts of Solomon and the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel and of Judah, but not its writer. The Talmud credits it to Jeremiah, and its last chapters are repeated as Jeremiah 52. It ends with Jehoiachin released in Babylon in the thirty-seventh year of his exile (≈561 BC, counted from his surrender in 597), so its last words were written after that. Martin Noth read it as the close of the Deuteronomistic History.

sources.note: repeats 2 Kings 24:18–25:30

sources.title: Überlieferungsgeschichtliche Studien
sources.author: Martin Noth
sources.note: Joshua to Kings as one Deuteronomistic History

traditions: Jeremiah: Talmudic tradition
Deuteronomistic History, finished in the exile: Martin Noth (1943) and those who follow him

name: Chronicles: anonymous (the Talmud says Ezra)
summary: Chronicles names no writer. The Talmud says Ezra wrote its genealogies down to his own time and Nehemiah finished it. Its last verses are the opening of Ezra, Cyrus's decree, and its line of David runs on several generations past Zerubbabel, so it was finished well after the return. Critical scholars date it to the late Persian or early Greek period, and some, Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson among them, do not think one writer produced both it and Ezra–Nehemiah.

sources.title: The Supposed Common Authorship of Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah Investigated Anew
sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.note: Vetus Testamentum 18

traditions: Ezra, finished by Nehemiah: Talmudic tradition
An anonymous 'Chronicler' after the return: modern critical scholarship

name: Ezra the scribe
summary: From 7:27 to the end of chapter 9 Ezra tells his own story in the first person, and the Talmud says Ezra wrote his own book. The rest is told about him, and quotes Persian letters and decrees in Aramaic (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26). The Hebrew Bible counts Ezra and Nehemiah as one book.
traditions: Ezra: Talmudic and traditional view
Compiled later from Ezra's memoir and official documents: modern critical scholarship

name: Nehemiah son of Hacaliah
summary: 'The words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah' (1:1): much of the book is his memoir in the first person, ending 'Remember me, O my God, with favor.' The Talmud treats it as part of Ezra's book and says Nehemiah finished Chronicles. Critical scholars take an editor to have joined his memoir to the rest.
traditions: Nehemiah, as part of the book of Ezra: Talmudic view
His memoir, joined to other material by an editor: modern critical scholarship

name: Esther: writer unknown
summary: The book names no writer. It says Mordecai recorded these events and sent letters to the Jews, and that Esther and Mordecai wrote with full authority to confirm Purim. The Talmud credits the book to the men of the Great Assembly. Critical scholars date it to the Persian or early Greek period.
traditions: The men of the Great Assembly: Talmudic tradition
An unknown writer of the Persian or Greek period: modern critical scholarship

name: Job: writer unknown
summary: The book names no writer and gives no date. The Talmud says Moses wrote it, and records rabbis who placed Job in the days of Moses, of Israel in Egypt, or of the return from Babylon, and one who held that 'Job never existed... his story was a parable.' Critical scholars date it from its language to between the seventh and fourth centuries BC.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b (who wrote the books)

traditions: Moses: Talmudic tradition
An unknown writer of the seventh to fourth centuries BC: modern critical scholarship

name: No heading names a writer
summary: Fifty psalms have no heading naming anyone. The New Testament credits two of them to David: Psalm 2 ('through the mouth of Your servant, our father David') and Psalm 95 ('He spoke through David'). The Talmud says David wrote the Psalms 'by means of ten elders', among them Adam, Melchizedek and Abraham.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b (who wrote the books)

name: David (psalm superscriptions)
heading: of David
summary: 73 psalms carry the heading 'of David' (le-David). The Hebrew preposition can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of', so the heading is read both as authorship and as a label. The New Testament cites Psalms 2, 16, 32, 69, 95, 109 and 110 as David's. Other named contributors are Asaph (12), the sons of Korah (11), Solomon (2), Moses (1), Heman and Ethan (1 each).

sources.note: the first Davidic heading
'the sweet psalmist of Israel'
'A prayer of Moses'

traditions: Headings as authorship: traditional reading
Headings as later collection labels: critical scholarship, some of which allows Davidic origin for some psalms

name: The sons of Korah (psalm headings)
heading: of the sons of Korah
summary: Eleven psalms are headed 'of the sons of Korah'. Korah son of Izhar died in his revolt against Moses, but 'the line of Korah did not die out'; Chronicles has Korahites guarding the tent's thresholds and standing up to praise the LORD in Jehoshaphat's day. Read as a label, the heading names a family of Levite singers, not one writer.
traditions: Heading as authorship: traditional reading
Heading as the name of a guild or collection: much critical scholarship

name: Asaph (psalm headings)
heading: of Asaph
summary: Twelve psalms are headed 'of Asaph'. Chronicles names Asaph son of Berechiah among the Levites David set over the singing, and has Hezekiah's Levites praise 'in the words of David and of Asaph the seer'. Some of these psalms mourn the temple burned (74:7), four centuries after him, which is one reason given for reading the heading as the name of the singers descended from him, 'the descendants of Asaph' of the return.
traditions: Heading as authorship: traditional reading
Heading as the name of a guild or collection: much critical scholarship

name: Solomon (psalm headings)
heading: of Solomon
summary: Psalms 72 and 127 are headed 'of Solomon'. Psalm 72 prays for 'the son of the king' and ends 'Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse', so its heading may mean 'for Solomon'. Kings says Solomon's songs numbered a thousand and five.
traditions: Heading as authorship: traditional reading
Heading as the name of a guild or collection: much critical scholarship

name: Heman the Ezrahite (Psalm 88)
heading: of Heman the Ezrahite
summary: Psalm 88 has two headings, 'of the sons of Korah' and 'of Heman the Ezrahite'. Kings names a Heman among the wise men Solomon surpassed, one of the sons of Mahol; Chronicles names Heman son of Joel as one of David's chief singers, and a Heman among the sons of Zerah. The Talmud asks whether there were two Hemans. STEPBible's data takes the psalm's Heman for the wise man of Kings.
traditions: Heading as authorship: traditional reading
Heading as the name of a guild or collection: much critical scholarship

name: Ethan the Ezrahite (Psalm 89)
heading: of Ethan the Ezrahite
summary: Psalm 89 is headed 'of Ethan the Ezrahite', the wise man Kings names first among those Solomon surpassed. It sets God's covenant with David beside its apparent failure ('You have renounced the covenant with Your servant'). In the Talmud, Rav identified Ethan with Abraham.
traditions: Heading as authorship: traditional reading
Heading as the name of a guild or collection: much critical scholarship

name: Moses (Psalm 90)
heading: of Moses
summary: 'A prayer of Moses the man of God' heads Psalm 90, the only psalm given his name, which opens the fourth book of the Psalter. Its plea that the LORD turn and relent (90:13) uses the two Hebrew verbs of Moses' own plea after the golden calf. The Talmud counts Moses among the ten elders whose psalms David gathered.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b (who wrote the books)

traditions: Heading as authorship: traditional reading
Heading as the name of a guild or collection: much critical scholarship

name: Solomon and others
summary: The book names its hands: the proverbs of Solomon (1:1; 10:1), 'the words of the wise' (22:17; 24:23), Solomon's proverbs 'copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah' (25:1), and the words of Agur (30:1) and of King Lemuel (31:1). Kings says Solomon composed three thousand proverbs. The Talmud credits the writing down to Hezekiah and his colleagues. 22:17–24:22 runs closely parallel to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.

sources.title: Instruction of Amenemope, papyrus, British Museum EA 10474

name: 'The Teacher' (Qoheleth), traditionally Solomon
summary: 'The words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem' (1:1). The book never names Solomon, though the Teacher speaks as a king of Israel in Jerusalem (1:12) wiser and richer than all before him, and its close speaks of him in the third person (12:9–10). Jewish and Christian tradition took him for Solomon; the Talmud credits the writing down to Hezekiah and his colleagues. Critical scholars date it to the Persian or Greek period from its late Hebrew, which borrows Persian words (pardes, the 'parks' of 2:5).
traditions: Solomon: traditional Jewish and Christian view
A later sage writing in the voice of a king: modern critical scholarship

name: Solomon (title)
summary: 'This is Solomon's Song of Songs' (1:1). As with 'of David' in the psalms, the Hebrew can mean by, for or about Solomon, who appears in the poem (3:7; 8:11). Kings says his songs numbered a thousand and five. The Talmud credits the writing down to Hezekiah and his colleagues; critical scholars read it as a collection of love poems from the monarchy or later.
traditions: Solomon: traditional view
A collection of love poems, of uncertain date: modern critical scholarship

name: Isaiah of Jerusalem (and the question of chapters 40–66)
summary: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem c. 740–700 BC (1:1). Chapters 40–66 address the Babylonian exile and name Cyrus (44:28; 45:1), events 150 years later; since the eighteenth century critical scholars have attributed them to one or two later prophets writing in Isaiah's tradition ('Second' and 'Third Isaiah'). Traditional readers take the Cyrus passages as predictive. The Great Isaiah Scroll (c. 125 BC) already has all 66 chapters as one book.

sources.title: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ), Shrine of the Book
sources.note: 'The 54 columns contain all 66 chapters of the Hebrew version of the biblical Book of Isaiah. Dating from ca. 125 BCE'

sources.title: Sirach 48:22–25 (c. 180 BC)
sources.note: already credits Isaiah with comforting 'those who mourned in Zion' — chapters 40–66

traditions: Single author: traditional Jewish and Christian view, conservative evangelicalism
Two or three authors: critical scholarship since the eighteenth century, Catholic and Protestant

name: Jeremiah, through Baruch his scribe
summary: The book says Jeremiah dictated his prophecies to Baruch son of Neriah, who wrote them on a scroll; when King Jehoiakim burned it, Jeremiah dictated them again, 'and many similar words were added'. 'Here end the words of Jeremiah' (51:64): the last chapter is an appendix repeated from Kings. The Greek Septuagint is ≈ a seventh shorter and orders the oracles differently, and Hebrew copies of the shorter form were found at Qumran.

sources.title: Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible
sources.author: Emanuel Tov
sources.note: the two editions of Jeremiah, and 4QJer b and d

name: Lamentations: anonymous (traditionally Jeremiah)
summary: The five poems name no writer. The Greek translation opens with a line saying Jeremiah sat weeping and spoke this lament, the Talmud credits the book to him, and Chronicles says Jeremiah lamented over Josiah in laments still sung. Critical scholars take the poems, four of them alphabetic acrostics, to come from more than one hand in Judah after Jerusalem fell (≈586 BC).

sources.title: Septuagint, Lamentations 1:1 (the introductory sentence)
sources.note: Brenton's translation: 'Jeremias sat weeping, and lamented with this lamentation over Jerusalem'

traditions: Jeremiah: Greek and Talmudic tradition
Several anonymous poets after 586 BC: modern critical scholarship

name: Ezekiel son of Buzi
summary: Ezekiel, a priest taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin, tells the book in the first person and dates its oracles by the years of that exile, from the fifth (1:2) to the twenty-seventh (29:17). The Talmud says the men of the Great Assembly wrote it down. Critical scholars take the bulk as his, with later editing.

name: Daniel (and the question of its date)
summary: Chapters 1–6 tell of Daniel in the third person; in 7–12 he tells his visions in the first, and 7:1 says he 'wrote down the dream'. From 2:4 to the end of chapter 7 it is in Aramaic. Jesus speaks of 'the prophet Daniel'. The Talmud credits the men of the Great Assembly with writing it down. Critical scholars date the visions to ≈167–164 BC, because chapter 11 follows the wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids in detail down to Antiochus IV and then parts from what happened (11:40–45); the philosopher Porphyry argued this in the third century AD. Traditional readers hold that Daniel wrote in the sixth century BC and that chapter 11 is prophecy.

sources.title: Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, prologue (reporting Porphyry's argument)
sources.note: Gleason Archer's translation (1958): Porphyry denied the book 'was composed by the person to whom it is ascribed in its title, but rather by some individual living in Judaea at the time of the Antiochus who was surnamed Epiphanes'

traditions: Daniel in the sixth century BC: traditional Jewish and Christian view
Final form ≈167–164 BC, under Antiochus IV: Porphyry, and critical scholarship after him

name: Hosea son of Beeri
summary: 'The word of the LORD that came to Hosea son of Beeri' in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel (1:1). Chapter 1 tells of him in the third person, chapter 3 in the first. The Talmud credits the men of the Great Assembly with writing down the Twelve. Critical scholars take the oracles as his, from the eighth century BC, collected and edited in Judah.

name: Joel son of Pethuel
summary: 'The word of the LORD that came to Joel son of Pethuel' (1:1). The book names no king and gives no date, so it has been placed anywhere from the ninth century BC to the fourth: Keil and Delitzsch early, Hans Walter Wolff after the exile. The Talmud credits the men of the Great Assembly with writing down the Twelve.

sources.title: Joel and Amos (Hermeneia)
sources.author: Hans Walter Wolff
sources.note: dates Joel after the exile

sources.title: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament: The Twelve Minor Prophets, introduction to Joel
sources.author: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch)
sources.note: 'the first thirty years of the reign of Joash, during which the king had Jehoiada the high priest for his adviser, are to be regarded as the period of Joel's ministry'

name: Amos of Tekoa
summary: 'The words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa', two years before the earthquake, under Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash of Israel (1:1). 'I was not a prophet... I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees' (7:14). Its one story about him (7:10–17) is told in the third person.

name: Obadiah
summary: 'The vision of Obadiah' (1:1): nothing else is told of him. Emil Hirsch and George Barton date the book after Edom stood aloof while 'foreigners... cast lots for Jerusalem' (v. 11), taking that for Babylon's capture of the city (≈586 BC); Keil and Delitzsch date it under Jehoram.

sources.title: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament: Obadiah
sources.author: C. F. Keil and Franz Delitzsch
sources.note: 'there only remains the taking of Jerusalem by the Philistines and Arabians in the time of Jehoram'

sources.title: Obadiah, Book of
sources.author: Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton
sources.note: Jewish Encyclopedia: 'Ob. 11-14 seems clearly to refer to the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar (586 B.C.)'

sources.title: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament: The Twelve Minor Prophets, introduction to Obadiah
sources.author: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch)
sources.note: 'fix upon the reign of Joram as the date of his ministry'

name: Jonah: told about him, writer unknown
summary: The book tells of Jonah son of Amittai in the third person and does not say who wrote it. Kings places him in the reign of Jeroboam II, in the eighth century BC. Tradition has credited the book to Jonah; the Talmud credits the men of the Great Assembly with writing down the Twelve. Critical scholars date it after the exile.
traditions: Jonah: traditional view
An unknown writer after the exile: modern critical scholarship

name: Micah of Moresheth
summary: 'The word of the LORD that came to Micah of Moresheth' under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1). A century later, elders quoted his 'Zion will be plowed like a field' (3:12) at Jeremiah's trial. Chapters 1–3 are not disputed as his; critical scholars take parts of 4–7 to have been added later.
traditions: The whole book Micah's: traditional view
Chapters 1–3 his, much of 4–7 later: critical scholarship

name: Nahum the Elkoshite
summary: 'The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite' (1:1). It foretells Nineveh's fall and points to Thebes as already fallen (3:8), so on that reading it was written between Assyria's sack of Thebes (663 BC) and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC).

name: Habakkuk the prophet
summary: 'The burden that Habakkuk the prophet received' (1:1), with 'a prayer of Habakkuk the prophet' (3:1). It speaks of God raising up the Chaldeans (1:6), so it has been dated near the end of the seventh century BC. A commentary on its first two chapters is among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

sources.title: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), Dead Sea Scrolls, Shrine of the Book
sources.note: 'It interprets the first two chapters of the biblical book of the prophet Habakkuk'

name: Zephaniah son of Cushi
summary: 'The word of the LORD that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi', traced back four generations to a Hezekiah, perhaps the king, in the days of Josiah (1:1).

name: Haggai the prophet
summary: Four messages dated to the second year of Darius (≈520 BC, from Darius I's accession in 522), urging the rebuilding of the temple (1:1). The book speaks of Haggai in the third person.

name: Zechariah son of Berechiah (and chapters 9–14)
summary: Chapters 1–8 are Zechariah's dated visions, from the second year of Darius (1:1). Chapters 9–14 have no dates and a different style, under two headings of their own ('the burden of the word of the LORD', 9:1 and 12:1). Matthew quotes 11:12–13 under Jeremiah's name, and critical scholars attribute 9–14 to later hands ('Second Zechariah').
traditions: One prophet: traditional view
Chapters 9–14 by later hands: critical scholarship

name: Malachi ('my messenger')
summary: 'The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel through Malachi' (1:1). The name means 'my messenger', the word of 3:1, so it may be a title. In the Talmud, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa said Malachi was Ezra, while the Sages held that Malachi was his own name.
traditions: A prophet named Malachi: the Sages in the Talmud
Ezra: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
An anonymous prophet, the name taken from 3:1: some modern scholars

name: Tobit: writer unknown
summary: 'The book of the words of Tobit' (1:1) is told in Tobit's own voice until his prayer (3:6), then in the third person. Its writer is unknown. Four Aramaic copies and one Hebrew were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and it has been dated to the third or second century BC. Jerome noted that Tobit is 'not in the canon' of the Hebrew Bible.

sources.title: Tobit, 4Q196–200, Dead Sea Scrolls
sources.note: 4Q196 (papTobit) to 4Q200, each with its own page in the Leon Levy library

sources.title: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Samuel and Kings

name: Judith: writer unknown
summary: The book names no writer. It sets its story under 'Nebuchadnezzar, who reigned over the Assyrians in Nineveh' (1:1), though Nineveh had fallen before he reigned in Babylon, and it has been read as a story rather than a chronicle. It survives in Greek, and has been taken to be written in Hebrew in Judea in the second or first century BC.

name: Greek Esther: translated by Lysimachus
summary: For the Hebrew story, see Esther. The Greek ends with a note that in the fourth year of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus brought 'this letter of Purim', translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, of Jerusalem (10:14 here). Which Ptolemy is meant is debated (≈114 or ≈78/77 BC). The passages in square brackets, among them Mordecai's dream, the king's decrees and the prayers, have been taken to be written in Greek.

sources.title: The Colophon of the Greek Book of Esther
sources.author: Elias Bickerman
sources.note: Journal of Biblical Literature 63

name: Wisdom of Solomon: written in Solomon's voice
summary: The writer speaks as the king God chose and told to build a temple (9:7–8), praying for wisdom as Solomon does in Kings, but never names Solomon. The book was written in Greek, and has been placed in Alexandria between the first century BC and the early first century AD. The Muratorian fragment (c. AD 170–200) calls it 'written by the friends of Solomon in his honour'.

sources.title: Muratorian Fragment, lines 69–71
sources.note: Metzger's translation: 'the book of Wisdom, written by the friends of Solomon in his honour'

traditions: Solomon: some early readers
A Greek-speaking Jew of Alexandria writing in Solomon's name: the Muratorian fragment's 'friends of Solomon', and modern scholarship

name: Jesus son of Sirach (Ben Sira)
summary: The book signs itself: 'I Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem' (50:27). He wrote in Hebrew, praising the high priest Simon son of Onias (50:1), ≈190–175 BC. His grandson's prologue says he translated it into Greek after coming to Egypt in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (≈132 BC). Much of the Hebrew was recovered from the Cairo Genizah from 1896, and a scroll of chapters 39–44 at Masada.

sources.title: Prologue to Sirach, by the writer's grandson
Masada Ben Sira scroll (Mas1h), Israel Antiquities Authority
Ben Sira manuscripts from the Cairo Genizah, Taylor-Schechter Collection, Cambridge University Library

name: Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe (named)
summary: 'The words of the book which Baruch the son of Nerias... wrote in Babylon' (1:1): Jeremiah's scribe. Its parts differ in kind (a prose confession, a poem on wisdom, poems of comfort), and its confession (from 1:15) follows Daniel 9 closely, so critical scholars date the parts to the second or first century BC. Chapter 6, the Letter of Jeremiah, claims to be Jeremiah's; a Greek fragment of it was found at Qumran.

sources.title: Letter of Jeremiah in Greek, 7Q2, Dead Sea Scrolls

traditions: Baruch: the book's own claim, accepted in tradition
Several later writers in his name: modern critical scholarship

name: Greek Daniel's additions: writers unknown
summary: For the rest of the book, see Daniel. The Greek adds the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the Three (3:24–90 here), Susanna (chapter 13) and Bel and the Dragon (chapter 14), none of which the Hebrew–Aramaic book has. About AD 240 Julius Africanus argued to Origen that Susanna was composed in Greek, since Daniel's sentences pun on the trees the elders name (13:54–59), puns that work only in Greek; Origen replied defending the story.

name: 1 Maccabees: writer unknown
summary: The book names no writer. Jerome found 'the first book of Maccabees... to be Hebrew' and Origen gave its Hebrew title, but only the Greek survives. It ends with John Hyrcanus succeeding his father Simon (16:23–24), so it has been dated ≈100 BC.

sources.title: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Samuel and Kings

name: An abridger of Jason of Cyrene
summary: An unnamed writer says he has abridged into one book what 'Jason of Cyrene' told in five (2:23), and speaks in the first person in his preface (2:19–32) and close (15:37–39). Two letters to the Jews of Egypt stand before it (1:1–2:18), the first dated in the 188th year of the Seleucid era (1:9, ≈124 BC).

name: 1 Esdras: writer unknown
summary: A Greek retelling of the end of 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah 8, with one story the Hebrew lacks: the contest of Darius's three guards, which Zerubbabel wins (3:1–5:6). Its writer is unknown. Josephus follows it in his Antiquities, so it was in use by the first century AD.

sources.title: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 11.3
sources.note: Whiston's translation: the three guards' contest before Darius, which Zorobabel wins

name: Offered as the prayer of King Manasseh
summary: Chronicles says Manasseh humbled himself in captivity and prayed, and that 'his prayer to his God' is written in the records of the kings and of the seers (2 Chronicles 33:18–19). This prayer is offered as that one, but those records are lost and nothing ties this text to him. Its earliest witness is the Didascalia Apostolorum (third century AD); it has been dated between the second century BC and the first AD.

sources.title: Didascalia Apostolorum, chapter VII (3rd century)
sources.note: Connolly's translation (1929): Manasseh's story from Kings and Chronicles, with 'THE PRAYER OF MANASSEH' in full

traditions: Manasseh's own prayer: some Orthodox tradition
Written later in his voice: modern critical scholarship

name: David (by its Greek heading)
summary: The Greek heading calls it 'a genuine one of David, though extra, composed when he fought in single combat with Goliath'. A longer Hebrew form, in two poems, is in the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11, so the psalm is older than its Greek translation; who wrote it is unknown.

sources.title: Great Psalms Scroll (11Q5, 11QPsᵃ), Dead Sea Scrolls
sources.note: Psalm 151 in two poems (151a and 151b) at the scroll's end

traditions: David: the Greek heading
An unknown psalmist: modern scholarship

name: 3 Maccabees: writer unknown
summary: Despite its name it is not about the Maccabees: it tells of Ptolemy IV Philopator's persecution of the Jews of Egypt after the battle of Raphia (217 BC). Its writer is unknown; it was written in Greek, and has been placed in Alexandria in the first century BC.

name: 4 Maccabees: writer unknown (once credited to Josephus)
summary: A philosophical discourse that 'religious reasoning is absolute master of the emotions' (1:1), proved by the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7. Eusebius credited Josephus with a work 'On the Supremacy of Reason', which some called the Maccabaicum; modern scholars do not accept that, and date it to the first century AD.
traditions: Josephus: Eusebius
An unknown Greek-speaking Jew: modern scholarship

name: Written in Ezra's name ('I Salathiel, also called Esdras')
summary: Chapters 3–14 speak as 'I Salathiel, also called Esdras', in Babylon 'in the thirtieth year after the ruin of the city' (3:1). The writer mourns, under the figure of Babylon's capture of Jerusalem, its destruction by Rome in AD 70, and these chapters have been dated ≈AD 100. Chapters 1–2 and 15–16 are later Christian additions.
traditions: Ezra: the book's own claim
A Jewish writer about AD 100: modern scholarship

name: Written in Enoch's name
summary: 'The words of the blessing of Enoch' (1:1). Jude quotes 1:9 as the prophecy of 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam'. The book joins five works; Aramaic copies of four were found at Qumran, the oldest copied ≈200 BC, but none of the Similitudes (37–71). Its writers are unknown, and only the Ethiopian church reads it as Scripture.

sources.title: Aramaic Enoch, 4Q201–212, Dead Sea Scrolls (J. T. Milik, The Books of Enoch, 1976)

traditions: Enoch: the book's own claim, and the Ethiopian church's reading
Several unknown writers, third century BC to first century AD: modern scholarship

name: Dictated to Moses by an angel (its own claim)
summary: Jubilees presents itself as what the angel of the presence told Moses on Sinai, at God's command to 'write for Moses from the beginning of creation' (1:26 here, Charles's 1:27). It retells Genesis and Exodus to Sinai in a calendar of jubilees. Over a dozen Hebrew copies were found at Qumran, and its writing has been dated to ≈160–150 BC. Only the Ethiopian church reads it as Scripture.

sources.note: Charles's 1:27

sources.title: Jubilees, 4Q216 and other copies, Dead Sea Scrolls

traditions: Moses, by an angel's dictation: the book's own claim, and the Ethiopian church's reading
An unknown writer about 160–150 BC: modern scholarship

name: Matthew (traditional attribution)
summary: The Gospel is anonymous; the title 'According to Matthew' was attached by the early second century. Papias (c. AD 110, quoted by Eusebius) says Matthew 'compiled the sayings in the Hebrew dialect'. Critical scholars, Davies and Allison among them, take the Greek Gospel to have been written c. AD 70–90 by a Jewish-Christian author using Mark, not directly by the tax collector; the attribution is early and unanimous but not self-attested.

sources.title: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1
sources.note: 'Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him'
the call of Matthew the tax collector

sources.title: The Gospel According to Saint Matthew (ICC)
sources.author: W. D. Davies & Dale C. Allison

traditions: Apostolic authorship: traditional Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical view
Anonymous Jewish-Christian author dependent on Mark: critical scholarship (Davies and Allison)

name: Mark (John Mark), from Peter's preaching
summary: Papias, via Eusebius, says Mark was Peter's 'interpreter' and wrote down what Peter taught, 'though not in order'. The Gospel itself is anonymous. Its Latinisms and explanations of Jewish customs have been taken to suggest a Roman or at least non-Judean audience, and it has been dated c. AD 65–75.

sources.note: 'Mark, my son' with Peter in 'Babylon'

traditions: Mark, from Peter's preaching: Papias, as Eusebius quotes him

name: Luke, companion of Paul
summary: Luke–Acts is a single two-volume work addressed to Theophilus. Its author is unnamed but the 'we' passages in Acts place him with Paul; tradition since the second century identifies him with 'Luke the beloved physician' of Colossians 4:14. The Muratorian fragment and Irenaeus both name him.

sources.note: first 'we' passage

name: 'The disciple whom Jesus loved'
summary: The Gospel claims to rest on the testimony of the beloved disciple (21:24), whom it never names. Irenaeus identifies him with John the apostle, writing at Ephesus; some ancient and modern readers have proposed another John ('the Elder' whom Papias mentions). The final chapter speaks in the plural: 'we know that his testimony is true'.

sources.title: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1
sources.note: 'Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him'

sources.note: 'what things Aristion and the presbyter John, the disciples of the Lord, say'

traditions: Apostle John: traditional view
John the Elder or a Johannine school: critical scholars (Richard Bauckham argues for John the Elder as an eyewitness)

name: Paul of Tarsus
summary: Thirteen letters name Paul as sender. Seven are undisputed (Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon). Ephesians, Colossians and 2 Thessalonians are debated; the Pastorals (1–2 Timothy, Titus) are held by critical scholars, I. Howard Marshall among them, to be by a later follower, on grounds of vocabulary, church structure and chronology. Paul dictated to a secretary (Romans 16:22) and signed in his own hand (Galatians 6:11).

sources.note: 'I, Tertius, who wrote this letter'
Paul's letters already collected and called 'Scriptures'

traditions: All thirteen Pauline: traditional and evangelical view
Seven undisputed, six deutero-Pauline: critical scholarship

name: Hebrews: author unknown
summary: The letter names no author. Origen wrote, 'who wrote the epistle, in truth God knows'. Candidates proposed since antiquity include Paul, Barnabas (Tertullian), Apollos (Luther), Luke, Clement of Rome and Priscilla (Harnack). Origen himself found its style unlike Paul's.

sources.title: Tertullian, On Modesty 20
sources.note: attributes it to Barnabas: 'there is extant withal an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas'
the author knows Timothy

name: James, the brother of Jesus (traditional attribution)
summary: 'James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ' (1:1). Tradition identifies him with James the Lord's brother, who led the church in Jerusalem. Eusebius counted the letter among the disputed books, noting that 'not many of the ancients have mentioned it'. Some scholars think it was written in his name later, citing its polished Greek; others accept it as his.
traditions: James the brother of Jesus: traditional and conservative scholarship
Written in his name later: some critical scholars

name: Peter, through Silvanus
summary: 'Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ' (1:1), writing 'through Silvanus' (5:12), which may mean Silvanus drafted or carried it. Eusebius says it was 'acknowledged as genuine' and the ancient elders used it freely. Some critical scholars think it was written in Peter's name, citing its fluent Greek.
traditions: Peter, perhaps with Silvanus: traditional view
Written in Peter's name: some critical scholars

name: Peter (disputed since antiquity)
summary: 'Simon Peter' (1:1) claims to have been an eyewitness of Jesus' majesty on the holy mountain (1:16–18) and calls this his second letter (3:1). Eusebius wrote that 'his extant second Epistle does not belong to the canon', though many found it profitable. Critical scholars think it was written in his name, citing its reuse of Jude and its reference to Paul's letters as a collection (3:15–16).
traditions: Peter: traditional view
Written in Peter's name: critical scholarship

name: John (1 John anonymous; 2–3 John from 'the elder')
summary: 1 John names no writer, but claims to have seen and touched 'the Word of life' (1:1); 2 and 3 John are from 'the elder'. Irenaeus quotes 1 John as the letter of 'John, the disciple of the Lord'. Eusebius lists 2 and 3 John among the disputed books, 'whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name'. All three share the vocabulary of John's Gospel.
traditions: John the apostle: traditional view
John the Elder, or the 'Johannine community': some critical scholars

name: Jude, the brother of James
summary: 'Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James' (1). Tradition identifies him with Judas, one of the brothers of Jesus named in Mark 6:3. The letter quotes 1 Enoch as the prophecy of 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam' (14–15). Eusebius counted it among the disputed books.
traditions: Jude the brother of Jesus: traditional view
Written in his name: some critical scholars

name: John on Patmos ('I, John')
summary: The writer calls himself John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8), exiled on Patmos, but never an apostle. Justin Martyr, about AD 155, names him 'John, one of the apostles of Christ'. In the third century Dionysius of Alexandria judged from its Greek that it was not by the Gospel's writer, though he 'could not venture to reject the book'. Later readers divide between the apostle and another John.
traditions: John the apostle: traditional view
Another John, a Christian prophet of Asia: Dionysius of Alexandria, and some critical scholars
